title: Light direction — Image Wiki
text:
Light direction
  Where the light sits relative to the subject and to the camera. It decides where the shadows land and how much of the shaded side you get to see, which is what makes a flat picture look solid.

  
    Termlight direction
    Also calledlighting angle, key light position, light placement
    Not the same ashard and soft light, fill level, light falloff
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happensThe walk aroundWhy under-lighting reads as wrongCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Photograph the same face twice without moving the camera. Once with the window in front of them, once with the window to their left. Nothing about the face has changed, and yet only in the second frame can you tell what shape the head is.
That is direction, the other half of Hard and soft light: hardness decides what shadow edges look like, direction decides where they land and whether you can see them at all.
Why it happens
Two angles do all the work, and only one of them is obvious.
Angle one: light to surface. A patch of skin facing the light square-on catches the full dose. Tilt it away and the dose per square millimetre falls with the cosine of the tilt: 87% at 30°, 50% at 60°, 17% at 80°, nothing at 90°.



Figure by Scratchapixel, Diffuse and Lambertian Shading, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Source.
One beam of light, same width and same power in all three positions; only the angle at which it meets the grey plane changes. On the left it stands square-on and its footprint is the size of the beam itself. In the middle it is tilted, and the footprint has grown: the yellow core is the patch of surface (dA), the green fringe is the extra floor the tilt added, and the whole ellipse is the beam's oblique footprint (dL). Brightness is the ratio of the two — dA over dL (SRC-095) — so it drops as the fringe grows. On the right the beam is nearly flat along the plane and has almost stopped landing on it at all.
The numbers above are that ratio. Nothing is absorbed anywhere in the series: the shaded side of every ball, every apple and every cheek is dark purely because the same light was made to cover more surface.


But that is not what you see. Vision compresses the bright end, so apparent brightness falls far more gently: the same tilts look roughly 94%, 73% and 45% as bright. Both rows are true of different quantities, and mixing them up is why calculated shading often looks wrong.
Either way the shape of the curve is the point: nearly flat for a long stretch, then a cliff. That is why a head under one light shows a large, fairly even lit region and then a fast dark band, instead of a smooth ramp across the face. The names for the parts of that sequence are in The anatomy of a shadow.
Angle two: light to camera. The one people miss, and the one that decides whether an image looks three-dimensional. Every lit object has a shaded side; whether the picture conveys form depends on how much of that side is turned toward you.



Walker Evans, Allie Mae Burroughs, Hale County, Alabama, 1936. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division. Public domain.
This is what a light beside the lens does. Hunt for a shadow and you will find almost nothing to hold: a short one under the nose, a thin one under the chin and the lower lip, a faint darkening where the neck meets the collar. The clapboard wall behind her — the one surface in frame that could receive a cast shadow — carries none, so the light was close to the axis the camera is looking down.
Every surface the camera can see is a surface the light can see, so the shadows hide directly behind the things casting them. Notice what survives and what does not: the texture of the boards and the freckles is fully described, and the form of the head is not. Cheekbones, brow and jaw are stated by their outlines and by tone changes in the skin, not by shading. It is a portrait of a surface.


Form appears only when a share of the visible surface goes dark — when you see both sides of one object at once. Which is why a fill light gets parked next to the lens on purpose: its job is to open shadows without adding shape of its own.
The walk around

front, on the lensno form45° up and acrossform + texture90°, straight sidehalf loststraight overheadraccoon eyesfrom belowreads wrong

One ball, one lamp, five positions. Follow the terminator — the boundary between lit and unlit — as the lamp travels. With the lamp on the lens the terminator is pushed right round onto the silhouette, so nearly the whole visible surface is lit and there is nothing left to read the shape from. At 45° it cuts a diagonal and you get a lit side and a shaded side in the same view: this is where form appears.
At 90° it lands exactly on the vertical centre line and half the object is gone. Overhead it lies flat across the middle, which on a face is what puts the eye sockets in the dark. From below the whole pattern is inverted — nothing is physically broken, and that is the point: every shadow is simply where your visual system does not expect one.


What each position is for:

On axis. Passport photos and on-camera flash. Cambridge in Colour is blunt: frontal light destroys a portrait's sense of depth.
45° across and 45° up. A small triangle of light appears on the far cheek, under the eye — the tell for Rembrandt lighting. Tall and wide means the light drifted frontward; thinned out means it went too far round, and the nose shadow is heading for the mouth.
90°, straight side. Half the information is gone unless something fills it. Texture peaks here.
Behind the subject. The front drops into shadow and a rim appears along hair and shoulders. Pushed slightly behind a profile rather than dead sideways, the head keeps its shape.
Overhead. Realistic, since the sun and every office ceiling do it, but Roger Deakins had the top light removed from the characters in How to Train Your Dragon: a realistic source is not always the most useful one on a face.
Below. Everything inverts, which is the next section.




Alfred T. Palmer, Operating a hand drill at Vultee-Nashville, Tennessee, February 1943. Library of Congress FSA/OWI Collection. Public domain.
Compare this with the Evans portrait: one light, moved off the axis. Start where the checklist below starts. There is a cast shadow here — the head's, thrown onto the yellow panel behind and to her right, with an edge you can trace — so the source sits out of frame to the camera's left, at about head height, and it is small enough to draw a hard edge.
Now look at what that bought. The eye socket is a distinct pocket of shade under a lit brow; there is a shadow beside the nose and another under the cheekbone; the far side of the jaw goes down into halftone while the front of the face stays lit. Every one of those is a piece of the face turned away from a light that is off to one side — the shaded fraction the frontal portrait had none of, and the reason the head reads as a solid object rather than a surface.


Why under-lighting reads as wrong
You have spent your whole life under light from above: sun, sky, ceiling lamps, streetlights. Your visual system leans on that hard enough to guess with — an ambiguous shaded blob reads as a bump or a dent partly on the grounds that the light is probably overhead.
Light a face from below and every shadow lands where nothing expects one. Nothing is broken, and yet the face reads as unfamiliar and faintly threatening — the torch-under-the-chin trick from every campfire ghost story, and why films light monsters this way. It stops feeling wrong the instant the frame explains it: a campfire, a laptop screen, a stove burner, footlights.



Gerrit van Honthorst, A Boy Blowing on a Firebrand, 1621–22 (Art Institute of Chicago). Public domain.
The source is in the picture, held below his chin, and everything follows from that position. Work upward from the firebrand: the underside of the nose is the brightest part of the face, the upper lip and the shelf of the chin catch light, and the shadow of the nose runs up onto the cheek instead of down. His brow is lit from beneath, so the ridge that normally shades the eyes is now shading the forehead above them.
The plume in his hat settles it: it is lit along its lower edges and dark on top. This is the direction that reads as sinister when nothing explains it, and here it reads as an ordinary boy with an ordinary ember, because the ember is in frame doing the work.



Reading the direction back out of an image
The catchlight tells you. Find the small bright reflection in someone's eye: it is a mirror image of the source, so where it sits on the eyeball points straight back at the lamp. High and to the left in the eye means the light was high and to the left. Two catchlights means two sources, and both should agree with every shadow in the frame.

Common mistakes

"Frontal light is the safe choice." Safe against ugly shadows, and it throws away more information than any other position: no form, no depth, and often a subject that flattens into its background's value mass (Value structure).
"Find the light by looking at the cast shadows." Not enough alone. Cast shadows point away from the light, the terminator runs across it, the catchlight points back at it. Check all three — in a composited or generated image, they are exactly what disagree.
"Side light is dramatic." Direction sets where the shadow is; how dark it goes is a separate control. A 90° key with heavy fill is gentle, a 45° key with none is brutal.
"Under-lighting is a mistake." Only when nothing in the frame produces it.
"Moving the light changes the direction." It changes direction, softness and brightness at once. See Hard and soft light and Light falloff, and check the result against The anatomy of a shadow.


How to read direction in five seconds

Find one clear cast shadow. Which way does it point? That is the direction in plan view.
Find a curved surface and locate the terminator. It should run roughly across that direction.
Find an eye, a chrome fitting, any glossy thing. Does the catchlight sit where the first two answers predict?
Ask what in the scene is making this light, and whether it is where it would have to be.
